opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's actually the most important existence proof we have. When we did Picbreeder, we saw these remarkably well-organized representations, where the skull image had a part of the network that controlled the mouth opening and closing, symmetry was built in, things were cleanly separated. But in Picbreeder there were humans in the loop making the selections, so a fair critique is: maybe the humans are the secret sauce. Maybe you need human judgment, with its sense of what's interesting, to get those factored representations.

Then you look at nature and realize there's no human there. Nobody picked which organisms to keep. Yet look at what it produced: genomes with incredibly modular, hierarchical, reusable structure. You've got Hox genes laying out the body plan, regulatory networks you can tweak to get a longer limb or an extra segment without breaking everything else. Evolution found a beautifully factored encoding of something as complex as a human being, and the encoding is evolvable in sensible ways. That's exactly the property we're excited about.

So what replaced the human? I'd argue it's the open-ended dynamics of the process itself. Evolution isn't optimizing toward a single objective. It's divergent. It keeps branching, finding new niches, accumulating stepping stones. Organisms are constrained by having to survive and reproduce, but that's a minimal criterion, not a target. In that kind of process, lineages whose representations are well-organized can keep producing viable, interesting variations, so over deep time the process favors evolvability. The good representations come along for the ride because they're what lets you keep discovering.

That's the lesson for algorithms. The question isn't "do we need humans?" It's "can we capture what humans and nature have in common?" Both explore without a fixed objective and both accumulate a growing archive of stepping stones. If we build algorithms that are open-ended in that way, rather than just pushing gradient descent toward a target, I think there's good reason to believe unified, factored representations can emerge without anyone choosing. Nature already did it once at an astonishing scale, so we know it's possible in principle.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing that strikes me about evolution is that it's a search process with no one in the loop. There's no human sitting there saying "this gene looks promising, keep it," and yet it produced brains, eyes, immune systems, the whole catalogue of life. And if you look at what evolution actually produced, the representations inside those systems are, in a sense, extraordinarily well factored. Your genome doesn't encode a separate program for each finger. It encodes something like "finger," and then reuses it with variations. Symmetry is a single regularity that gets applied across the whole body plan. That's exactly the kind of unified, modular, compressed representation that we struggle to get out of our own algorithms.

So the question for me was always: why did that happen? And I think the answer is that it wasn't a lucky accident. Evolution is not just searching for something that works; it's searching in a way that's constantly producing novelty and diversity, and over enormous timescales the things that survive and get built upon are the things that are easy to build upon. A tangled, spaghetti representation can't be modified gracefully, so it's a dead end in the search. A factored one can be tweaked a little and still function, and now you have a slightly different creature. So there's this implicit pressure, not for performance on a task, but for evolvability, for representations that support continued exploration. And that pressure emerges from the structure of open-ended search itself, not from anyone's judgment.

That's what gives me hope on the algorithmic side. In Picbreeder we needed humans in the loop to make the selections because we didn't know how to get that kind of divergent, serendipitous search any other way. But evolution tells us that humans aren't necessary in principle. There is some process, some set of ingredients, that generates this kind of order spontaneously. We just haven't captured it yet. And I don't think the missing piece is a cleverer objective. If anything, the lesson from nature is that the moment you fix a single objective and optimize hard against it, you lose exactly the property that makes the representations beautiful. So the challenge is to figure out what the algorithmic analogue of open-endedness is, something that keeps producing stepping stones that are interesting and reusable, without us having to be the ones who notice they're interesting.

r001.rationale: The response connects evolution to algorithmic search and hopes for an algorithmic analogue, but does not propose that large neural networks could learn these representations by incorporating evolutionary principles without being evolutionary algorithms.

r002.rationale: It describes reusable patterns such as fingers and symmetry, but does not identify preservation of structural regularities across generations as indirect evidence about representations underlying biological development.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention canalization or explain how developmental pathways preserve regularities despite mutations.

r004.rationale: It presents evolution as a human-free, open-ended search that produced highly factored biological representations, and argues this shows such order can emerge without a fixed objective or human selection.

astra-6.text:
Well, evolution is interesting because it gives us an existence proof. Our brains arose through an evolutionary process, and our brains can discover abstractions and recognize that the same underlying concept applies in very different situations. Evolution didn’t need a human standing outside the process saying, “That’s a good representation; keep that one.” Whatever machinery makes that possible emerged along the way.

Now, there’s an important distinction here: evolution didn’t directly encode every concept we have. It produced a system that can learn those concepts. So the lesson isn’t necessarily that we should evolve representations directly. It’s that an algorithmic process can discover the conditions under which powerful representations develop, without us specifying their structure in advance.

And of course evolution involves selection. The point is that it isn’t human selection, and it isn’t selection against a target representation. There was no explicit objective saying, “Produce a brain with unified, factored representations.” Yet something capable of that appeared. That makes me skeptical of the assumption that we have to understand and prescribe every intermediate step before an algorithm could get there.

r004.rationale: It presents evolution as an existence proof: without human selection or an objective specifying unified, factored representations, evolution produced brains capable of discovering abstractions that apply across different situations.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, evolution is an existence proof that you don’t need somebody standing outside the process, deciding which representations ought to be built. It starts with no understanding of the world, and eventually produces brains that can discover regularities, separate out different factors, and use what they’ve learned across many different situations.

Of course, there’s selection in evolution. But that’s different from a human choosing each intermediate step because it looks like progress toward intelligence. Nobody selected organisms for being a stepping stone to human thought. They survived and reproduced in their own environments, and along the way this extraordinary capacity emerged.

That doesn’t tell us exactly which algorithm will produce the representations we want. But it does undermine the idea that a human has to recognize and reward every important advance. A process can discover useful structure without anyone knowing in advance what that structure should be.
